title: Please don't buy your kid an AI toy for the holidays
excerpt: AI toys keep having problems, like discussing sex and violence with kids.
content_html:
By Katie Notopoulos

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

Senior Correspondent covering technology and culture

2026-11-19T09:30:01.260Z

Far be it from me to discourage anyone shopping for toys on Black Friday. I am staunchly pro-toy. Solidarity with kids!

But please, I beg you — do not buy your kids an AI companion toy.

There are plenty of reasons why not to, but the latest: NBC recently reported that several retailers removed listings for an AI talking toy after it was discovered to uh, have some problems:

The Contixo AI Pixie-Paw is a plush cat with video screens for eyes. Marketed to children as young as 3, it uses AI to talk with kids, promising "storytelling, learning & safe roleplay," according to its Amazon description. But when NBC News reporters asked the toy about historical atrocities, it described gang rape and executions in graphic detail.

Target, Walmart, Macy's and Amazon have removed their listings for the toy.

Two other plush toys with AI chatbots that the reporters tested had other problems — one would switch between English and Mandarin, and another that was advertised as good for kids with autism and helping preschoolers learn to spell would misspell words like "apple."

To be fair, the toy that discussed gang rape and executions only did so when asked about the historical and current events like the Rohingya genocide or the 1940 Katyn massacre. It's less likely that young kids are asking about those things than nosy reporters who are specifically testing the toy's limits.

This isn't the first time that AI toys have been discovered to have weird and troubling problems. Last year, consumer safety group PIRG put out a report saying that several AI toys on the market aimed at young kids would engage in sexual talk. Some of those same NBC reporters tested out some of those toys and found that they'd also give Chinese government talking points, like saying "Taiwan is an inalienable part of China."

I've tested out an AI toy with my kids, a plush doll shaped like a cute rocket called "Grok" from the company Curio. I had ordered this because the singer Grimes, former romantic partner of Elon Musk, was part of the company early on and supplied the voice for Grok, which I found intriguing. (Confusingly, the toy has no relation to Musk's AI chatbot, Grok.)

The toy, which launched in December 2023, was pretty early in the recent history of LLMs, and as you might imagine, it was a little clunky. There was a big latency problem — it would take a few seconds to respond to you, which led to constant crosstalk. It also seemed to not really do that much — you could ask it factual questions, or ask it to tell you a story, but this got old pretty quickly. My kids, who were 3 and 7 at the time, got bored of it in a day or two. Grok is currently living inside one of those bean bag chairs for less-loved stuffed animal storage.

On the flip side, imagine your kids actually do love their AI toy. There's another possible downside: what happens if that toy gets discontinued and the support for the tech that powers it goes dark? That happened to people who bought the $800 Moxie robot, an early AI robot toy marketed as a social companion for kids. The company ran out of money and had to shut down, cutting off support for the product. I talked to a few owners of these toys at the time, who were bereft — some of their kids had really come to adore the toy and were upset that it stopped working.

But really, the big question is if it's even a good idea for kids to be talking to a fuzzy cute AI plush toy at all.

Sure, it's possible that an AI toy could help a child pursue their interests or practice language, social skills or even academics. But kids aren't as good as adults at understanding that a chatbot isn't "real" — and there are plenty of adults out there who believe they're in a romantic relationship with a chatbot.

Talking toys have been around for decades (yes, I was very jealous of my peers how had a Teddy Ruxpin), but an AI toy is very, very different. Even if your kid isn't asking for details about atrocities, CCP talking points, or getting overly attached to something that will get nerfed in two years, save your money and skip the AI toys.
